How this article was made The code on this page was written with the help of an AI assistant, and the explanations grew out of an in-depth conversation with AI, used to work through the topic step by step. Every number comes from code that was actually run, and the claims are checked against the original papers listed under Sources. Part 1. The problem What a model can read, and why text has to be cut up at all.

Type the same greeting five ways. GPT-4o does not receive letters. It receives these numbers: You type GPT-4o receives hello hello 24,912 · hello · hello 40,617 Hello Hello 13,225 · Hello · Hello 32,949 HELLO HEL 111,642 LO 2,699 Five spellings, five unrelated numbers, and HELLO is not even one piece. Every model does this, each with its own numbers: Text Gemma 3 Qwen2.5 Llama 3.2 hello 23,391 14,990 15,339 · hello 29,104 23,811 24,748 Hello 9,259 9,707 9,906 · Hello 26,352 21,927 22,691 HELLO 174,886 50,712 + 1,593 51,812 + 1,623 GPT-4o's tokenizer is called o200k_base. OpenAI's own library (tiktoken) lists it for GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-5, o1, o3 and o4-mini. This article says "GPT-4o" rather than "ChatGPT" because the tokenizer of the newest ChatGPT model is not published. The model never sees the letters. It sees a list of numbers, one per token. The program that cuts text into tokens and gives each one its number is the tokenizer. The rest of this page is about how that program is made and why it gives these results.
Computers already store text as numbers

Start at the very bottom. A computer only stores numbers. For text there is a world-wide agreement called Unicode: every character in every language has a fixed number (its code point), written like U+0068 for "h". To save it in a file, each code point is written as 1 to 4 bytes using a scheme called UTF-8. A byte is a small number from 0 to 255 (8 bits: 2 8 = 256 possible values). Char What Code point UTF-8 bytes Bytes h letter h U+0068 104 1 H capital H U+0048 72 1 (space) space U+0020 32 1 é e with accent U+00E9 195 169 2 ₹ rupee sign U+20B9 226 130 185 3 中 Chinese character U+4E2D 228 184 173 3 🙂 emoji U+1F642 240 159 153 130 4 🤦‍♂️ emoji made of 4 parts 4 code points 240 159 164 166 226 128 141 226 153 130 239 184 143 13 So "hello" on disk is the five bytes 104 101 108 108 111. Plain English letters are 1 byte each; accented letters, the rupee sign, Chinese and emoji take more. The face-palm emoji is really 4 characters joined together (face palm + an invisible "joiner" + male sign + a style marker), 13 bytes in total. Important for later: any text at all can be written with only 256 different byte values. That is why modern tokenizers start from bytes.
How UTF-8 turns a number into bytes (and back)

How does a code point like "U+20B9" relate to the bytes in a file? Short answer: only bytes are stored. "U+20B9" is never written in the file; it is just how people write the character's number. UTF-8 is the rule that turns that number into bytes, and back. 1. What "U+" and hexadecimal mean Normal counting is base 10: digits 0–9, and each position is worth 10× the one to its right (1, 10, 100…). So 104 = 1×100 + 0×10 + 4×1. Hexadecimal is base 16: it needs 16 digits, so after 9 it uses letters: Hex digit Value 0–9 0–9 A 10 B 11 C 12 D 13 E 14 F 15 Each position is worth 16× the one to its right: 1, 16, 256, 4,096… The letter h is number 104. 104 = 6 sixteens + 8 ones, so in hex it is 68. Unicode pads it to 4 digits and puts "U+" in front: U+0068. "U+" only means "this is a Unicode number, written in hex". The rupee sign ₹ is U+20B9. Reading it back: Hex digit 2 0 B 9 Worth 2 × 4,096 = 8,192 0 × 256 = 0 B × 16 = 176 9 × 1 = 9 Total: 8,377. U+20B9 and 8,377 are the same number written two ways. People like hex because each hex digit is exactly 4 switches (bits), which makes the next part tidy. 2. A byte is 8 on/off switches Each switch has a fixed worth: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. The byte's value is the sum of the switches that are on (1). All on is the biggest: 255. worth 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 104 0 1 1 0 1 0 0 0 104 = 64 + 32 + 8 worth 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 226 1 1 1 0 0 0 1 0 226 = 128 + 64 + 32 + 2 3. The first switches of each byte are a label UTF-8 uses the first few switches of every byte as a label. The rule: count the 1s before the first 0. That is how many bytes the character has. A byte starting with 10 is a continuation byte. Byte starts with Values Meaning 0 … 0–127 a whole character by itself 110 … 192–223 start of a 2-byte character 1110 … 224–239 start of a 3-byte character 11110 … 240–247 start of a 4-byte character 10 … 128–191 continuation of the character before it The value ranges are not extra rules; they come straight from the labels. Every byte that starts with 1110 lies between 11100000 = 224 and 11101111 = 239. Strictly, 192, 193 and 245–247 never appear in valid UTF-8: they would only encode numbers that fit in fewer bytes, or numbers past Unicode's last character (U+10FFFF). The label idea is what matters. Some real bytes and what their label says: Byte Switches Label Means 104 01101000 0 a whole character by itself 226 11100010 1110 start of a 3-byte character 130 10000010 10 continuation of the character before it 185 10111001 10 continuation of the character before it 168 10101000 10 continuation of the character before it 240 11110000 11110 start of a 4-byte character 226 = 1110 0010: three 1s then a 0, so "a 3-byte character starts here: me plus the next 2". 104 starts with 0: it is "h" on its own. 168 = 1010 1000 starts with 10: it can only continue a character, never start one. Python agrees; decoding byte 168 by itself gives the error 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xa8 in position 0: invalid start byte. 4. The template: pour the number into the free switches After the label, the remaining switches of each byte are empty slots, and the character's number is poured into them, in order. ₹ is 8,377. In switches that is 16 bits: 0010000010111001. A 3-byte character has exactly 16 free slots: 1110____ (4) + 10______ (6) + 10______ (6). Pour the bits in, 4 then 6 then 6 (orange = label, blue = the number): Number's bits 0010 000010 111001 Byte 1110 0010 | 10 000010 | 10 111001 Value 226 130 185 So ₹ is stored as the three bytes 226 130 185, and nothing else. Why 3 bytes and not 2? A 2-byte character has only 5 + 6 = 11 free slots, enough for numbers up to 2,047. ₹ (8,377) needs more, so it takes the 3-byte form (16 slots, up to 65,535). Most emoji are bigger still and take 4 bytes. 5. Reading it back The program reads 226. Label 1110: this character is 3 bytes. It checks the next two bytes (130, 185) start with 10. They do, so they belong to this character. It removes the labels and glues the leftover switches: 0010 + 000010 + 111001 = 8,377. It looks up 8,377 in the Unicode table: ₹. Picture a train. The first carriage carries a sign: "this train has 3 carriages" (label 1110). Every other carriage carries a sign: "I belong to the train in front" (label 10). The passengers in the free seats are the pieces of the number. 6. The bytes do not say which rule to use A file does not carry a label saying "I am UTF-8"; the program has to be told or assume it. Read the same three bytes 226 130 185 with the old Windows-1252 rule (one byte = one character) and you get â‚¹: byte 226 becomes â, 130 becomes ‚ (a low quote mark), 185 becomes ¹. That is the garbled text you sometimes see on websites. Why this matters for tokenizers: byte-level BPE works on these stored bytes, not on characters. A token can hold the first carriage without the ones behind it. That is why some tokens are half a character (the emoji pieces in section 11) and only make sense once joined with the next tokens.
What a language model needs from us

A language model does one job again and again: look at the pieces so far and give a score to every possible next piece, then pick one. That one fact forces two things: A fixed, finite list of pieces. The model's last step produces one score per entry of the list, so the list has to be decided before the model is built. This list is the vocabulary. Each piece has a position number in that list (its ID). Inside the model, ID k picks row k of a big table of learned numbers (the embedding table). That row is what the model actually works with. Real example, the small open model SmolLM-135M: its list has 49,152 entries and each row has 576 numbers, so the table holds 28,311,552 numbers. That is 21% of the whole model (134,515,008 numbers). In this model the same table is used both to read the input and to score the next piece (config: tie_word_embeddings = True). So the tokenizer must turn any text into IDs from a fixed list, and turn IDs back into the exact same text. Everything that follows is about how to choose that list.

There are three obvious choices for "a piece" (the first comes in two versions). I measured them all on the same 5,166,860 bytes of new children's stories (text the tokenizer never saw): Cut into Pieces needed Size of the list one piece per character 5,164,777 every possible character (150,000+) one piece per byte 5,166,860 256 whole words (letters only) 1,036,957 11,336+, never complete our subword tokenizer (8,000 merges) 1,270,131 8,256 GPT-4o's tokenizer 1,233,789 200,019 "Pieces needed" = how many IDs the model would receive for this text. "Size of the list" = how many different entries the list must contain. Option A1: one piece per character Each character (h, e, ₹, “, 🙂...) is one piece, so the text needs 5,164,777 pieces, one per character. The problem is the list: it must have an entry for every character that could ever appear. This one text uses only 79 different characters, but Unicode has well over 150,000, and any character missing from the list could not be written at all. Option A2: one piece per byte Here a piece is one byte, not one character. Every character is first written as its 1 to 4 bytes (section 2), and each byte becomes its own piece. So the pieces needed = the number of bytes in the text, 5,166,860, slightly more than the 5,164,777 characters, because 1,042 characters in this text take more than 1 byte. The most common one is the curly quote “, which is the 3 bytes 226 128 156 and so becomes 3 pieces: 226 128 156 Plain letters like h are 1 byte, so they are still 1 piece each. The gain: the list needs only 256 entries. That 256 is not a number of characters; it is the number of different values one byte can hold (8 switches = 2×2×2×2×2×2×2×2 = 256). Every character in every language is written with these same 256 values (several of them in a row for bigger characters), so a list of 256 can write any text and nothing is ever missing. The cost: the text gets long, one ID per byte. The model has to work through 5,166,860 steps instead of about 1,233,789 with GPT-4o's tokenizer, and spends effort on spelling instead of meaning. The GPT-2 paper notes that byte-level models "are not competitive with word-level" ones on large datasets. Option B: whole words Short sequences, but the list never ends. I built a word list from the 22,161,827 characters of training stories: 11,336 different words (2,740 of them seen only once). Then I checked new text against it: New text Words Not in the word list new children's stories 1,036,957 1,496 (0.14%) the BPE research paper 6,986 3,024 (43%) In new stories from the same kind of text only 0.14% of words are missing, and they are mostly names (Rina, Inky, Aaron, Boxy, Jan). But in the BPE paper's own text, 43% of the words are missing: "translation", "vocabulary", "subword", "segmentation". A word-level model simply cannot write a word that is not on its list. Real tokenizers would also need separate entries for every "dog", "dogs", "Dog", typo and name. Option C: pieces of words (subwords) The middle road: frequent words become one piece, rare words are spelled from smaller pieces, and in the worst case single bytes, so nothing is ever missing. Our own small tokenizer from Part 2 cuts those "missing" words like this: Sennrich · S en n ri ch translation · tr ans l ation subword · sub w ord Edinburgh · Ed in b ur g h hyperparameter · h y p er par am eter Tokenizers used by today's models (GPT, Llama, Qwen, Gemma) all use option C, built with a recipe called Byte Pair Encoding (BPE). The Hugging Face files of Qwen2.5, Llama 3.2 and Gemma 3 all say model type: BPE. Part 2. Training a tokenizer Where the list comes from.

Short answer: it is not like training an LLM. The word "training" only means the list is learned from example text instead of being written by hand. There is no neural network, no GPU and no guessing. It is counting. If you changed the list after training the model, every row would suddenly belong to a different piece and the model would read nonsense. So a model and its tokenizer are a fixed pair. The glitch-token paper (Land & Bartolo 2024) is about what goes wrong because the two are made separately: "the disconnect between tokenizer creation and model training". Order of events: 1. collect text → 2. train the tokenizer (counting, minutes to hours) → 3. freeze it → 4. turn all training text into IDs → 5. train the LLM on those IDs (the expensive part).
Step 0 in detail: chopping text into chunks before training

Before any counting, the text is cut into word-sized chunks by a fixed, hand-written rule. Merges are only ever counted inside a chunk, never across two chunks. Apart from the special tokens (section 12), this rule is the only part of a tokenizer that a person writes by hand; everything else is learned. 6a. Why bother? Experiment To see what step 0 does, I trained three small test tokenizers of my own, not real GPT-2. To keep it quick each one learned only 500 merges from the same 300,000 characters. (The real GPT-2 tokenizer has 50,000 merges; a small test is enough to show the effect.) The only difference between the three is the step-0 rule: none at all, splitting at spaces only, or GPT-2's chopping rule, the pattern GPT-2 uses before merging. The cost: a list full of entries that only make sense for this one kind of text, and pieces that do not line up with words. 6b. The second reason: speed Training happens in two stages: Once, at the start: one pass over the whole text. Cut it into chunks (step 0) and count how often each different chunk appears. The result is a dictionary of chunk → count. Our 5,411,109 chunks become only 13,119 different ones, because the same words repeat. The most common:. 421,616 times,, 235,432 times, · the 211,031 times, · and 196,057 times. Every merge round after that (8,000 rounds for our tokenizer) works only on the dictionary. To count pairs, it looks at each of the 13,119 entries once and adds its pairs count times. To glue the winning pair, it again only changes the 13,119 entries. Why this saves time. Take one chunk, ·the, which appears 211,031 times. In every round the program must count the pairs inside it ( ·t + he and so on). Without the dictionary it would read ·the 211,031 separate times and add 1 each time. With the dictionary it reads ·the once and adds 211,031 in one go. Same answer, one look instead of 211,031. The same happens for every chunk, in every round. The BPE paper does exactly this: "the algorithm can thus be run on the dictionary extracted from a text, with each word being weighted by its frequency". It only works because of step 0: merges never cross chunks, so two copies of the same chunk always change in exactly the same way, and one entry with a count can stand for all of them. 6c. The starting list is the 256 possible byte values. Every chunk is written as its bytes: ·hello = 32 104 101 108 108 111. Why bytes and not "all characters"? Why is it called "Byte Pair Encoding"? The name is older than AI. BPE started in 1994 as a way to compress files (Philip Gage, "A New Algorithm for Data Compression", C Users Journal). The BPE paper describes the original as "a simple data compression technique that iteratively replaces the most frequent pair of bytes in a sequence with a single, unused byte". So the name says exactly what it did: look at pairs of bytes side by side, and re-encode the file by replacing the most common pair with one new byte, making it shorter. Example: a file whose bytes are ABCABCABD (9 bytes). Each step replaces the most common pair with a byte the file never uses: Step Most common pair Seen Replace with Bytes after 1 AB 3 times Z ZCZCZD (6) 2 ZC 2 times Y YYZD (4) 9 bytes became 4, plus a small table (Z = AB, Y = ZC) to unpack it: replace in reverse order (Y becomes ZC → Z becomes AB) and you get back exactly ABCABCABD. In 2016 Sennrich and colleagues borrowed the same loop for language: glue the most frequent pair of characters to build a list of word pieces. The name stayed even though they worked on characters; the GPT-2 paper remarks that "despite its name, reference BPE implementations often operate on Unicode code points and not byte sequences". GPT-2 went back to real bytes, which is the version on this page. One difference: Gage could only use byte values the file did not already contain, and there are only 256. A tokenizer has no such limit: each merge simply gets the next new ID (256, 257, 258…), so the list can grow to 50,000 or 200,000 entries. The training loop The whole training loop: Look inside every chunk and count every pair of neighbouring pieces (each chunk counts as many times as it appears in the text). Take the pair with the highest count. Give the glued pair a new ID (the next free number) and add it to the list. Write down the rule. Everywhere that pair appears, replace it with the new piece. Go back to 1. Stop when the list reaches the chosen size. Each round adds exactly one entry. Pieces can grow by gluing two already-glued pieces (" t" + "he" → " the"). Ties are broken by a fixed rule so the result is repeatable. A tiny example, every step shown Text: the cat sat on the mat the cat ran After step 0 the chunks are: the, · cat ×2, · sat, · on, · the ×2, · mat, · ran. Note ·the appears twice, ·cat twice; the very first the has no space because nothing comes before it. Round 1, the counting. Encoding: turning your text into IDs

When you send a message, the tokenizer does not search for the longest matching word. It replays the training: Step 0 with the same rule: cut into chunks. Write each chunk as bytes. Look at every neighbouring pair; if a rule exists for it, apply the rule that was learned earliest. Repeat until no rule applies. In GPT-4o's tokenizer a piece's ID is also its rule's position in the learned order (lower ID = learned earlier; tiktoken's own reference code calls IDs "ranks" and says they "correspond to merge priority"). Decoding: turning IDs back into text

The reverse is simple: look up each ID's bytes, join all the bytes, read them as UTF-8. For IDs that came from encoding real text you always get back exactly the text you started with. One catch: a single piece can be half a character. GPT-4o writes the face-palm emoji (13 bytes) as 5 tokens: <20 · f0 · 9f · a4> 93,643 <a6> 99 ‍ 2,524 ♂ 178,729 ️ 15,148 The first and some middle pieces are just fragments of the emoji's bytes. Alone they are not valid text; only together do they decode to 🤦‍♂️. (This is also why one emoji can cost several tokens: GPT-4 uses 8 for it.) The decoding chain, step by step When a model produces token IDs, this is what turns them into text. Example: GPT-2 writes the curly quote “ as two tokens, IDs 447 + 250. Look up each ID's bytes in the tokenizer's list. A piece can be any number of bytes, not always a pair: ID 447 = bytes 226 128 (half a character), ID 250 = byte 156. "h" is 1 byte, "·hello" is 6. Join all the bytes into one row: 226 128 156. The UTF-8 reader walks along the row using the labels (section 2b): a byte starting with 0 is a character on its own; 110 means "me plus 1 more byte"; 1110 means "me plus 2 more" (226 is 1110 0010); every following byte must start with 10. Here 128 and 156 both do, so the three bytes give “. What if the model picks a token that does not finish the character? It can happen. The model picks one token at a time, and nothing inside it forces the bytes to fit together. Three things deal with it: 1. Usually the model continues correctly. In its training text the piece 226 128 was always followed by the rest of a character (156, 157, 153…), never by a letter, so it learns that very strongly. A wrong pick is rare, but not impossible. 2. If it happens, the decoder does not crash; it shows a replacement mark. Tested with GPT-2's real decoder (OpenAI's tiktoken): Token IDs Bytes Decoded text 447 + 250 (correct) 226 128 156 “ 447 + 71 (half piece, then h) 226 128 104 �h 447 (half piece alone) 226 128 � 447 + 251 (half piece, then 157) 226 128 157 ” Byte 104 ("h") starts with 0, not 10, so the reader knows the character was broken. It writes � (the official Unicode "replacement character") in place of the broken bytes and carries on normally with h. tiktoken does this by default (its decode has errors="replace", the same setting as minibpe.py in Part 6). In strict mode it stops with an error instead: 'utf-8' codec can't decode bytes in position 0-1: invalid continuation byte. 3. A different wrong pick can give a valid but different character. If the model picks byte 157 instead of 156 after 226 128, the bytes fit perfectly and you get ” instead of “. No error at all: that is just an ordinary wrong prediction, like picking the wrong word. While text streams in word by word, a program showing it receives the half piece 226 128 first. It cannot print anything yet, so it waits for the next token to finish the character. That is why a well-built chat app does not flash half a character; at worst you would see � if the model really did go wrong.

From an ID to a meaning

Each ID picks a row in the embedding table. Before training the rows are random. During training, pieces that are used in similar places get pushed towards similar rows, because that helps the model predict the next piece. Real check on SmolLM-135M. "Cosine" measures how similar two rows are (1 = same direction). How big should the list be?

Sizes in real tokenizers (measured from their files): Tokenizer Entries GPT-2 (2019) 50,257 GPT-4 (cl100k_base) 100,277 GPT-4o / GPT-5 (o200k_base) 200,019 Llama 3.2 128,000 + 256 added Qwen2.5 151,643 + 22 added Gemma 3 262,144 The trade-off: Bigger list → more words are one piece → shorter inputs (our curve in section 8), so more text fits in the model's context and each request is cheaper and faster. But every entry needs its own row of learned numbers (in SmolLM-135M the table is already 21% of the model), and the model must score every entry at every step. Rare entries are seen only a few times during model training, so their rows stay poorly trained. The extreme case is the glitch token (section 17). Part 5. Consequences Odd behaviour that comes straight from the tokenizer.

How "1234567" is cut: GPT-2 123 | 45 | 67; GPT-4 and GPT-4o 123 | 456 | 7 (their step 0 allows at most 3 digits, grouped from the left); Qwen2.5 and Gemma 3 one digit per token (the Gemma 3 report lists "split digits" as a design choice of its tokenizer). " 2024" is one token in GPT-2 but "202" + "4" in GPT-4. Research: Singh & Strouse 2024 tested GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on arithmetic and found that grouping digits from the right (forced by writing numbers with commas, 1,234,567) "leads to largely improved performance", and the errors with left-to-right grouping follow fixed patterns. They also note LLaMa and PaLM chose single-digit tokens.

The list is learned from example text, so languages that were rare in that text get few entries and are cut into many small pieces. Petrov et al. 2023 measured the same text translated into many languages: tokenized lengths differ "up to 15 times in some cases", and even byte-level models show "over 4 times the difference" for some pairs. That means higher cost, slower answers and less room in the context window for those users.

"·SolidGoldMagikarp" is a single entry in GPT-2's list (so it was frequent in the text the tokenizer was trained on), but almost never appeared in the text the model was trained on. So its row was barely trained. The paper says such inputs can "induce unwanted model behaviour". Land & Bartolo 2024 define these as "tokens present in the tokenizer vocabulary but that are nearly or entirely absent during model training" and found them across many models. In GPT-4 and GPT-4o the same string is 5 pieces (GPT-4o's step 0 already cuts it at the capital letters).

BPE (Sennrich et al. 2016, from a 1994 compression trick): start small, glue the most frequent pair. Used by GPT, Llama, Qwen, Gemma. WordPiece: used by BERT (2018) with a 30,000-token list. Also builds pieces of words; how it picks them differs from BPE. Unigram (Kudo 2018): the opposite direction. Start with a "reasonably big seed vocabulary", then repeatedly remove the pieces whose removal hurts the least, keeping the top 80% each round, until the target size; single characters are always kept so nothing is missing. SentencePiece (Kudo & Richardson 2018): a toolkit, not a fourth algorithm. It can train BPE or Unigram directly on raw text, with the "▁" space marker.

API prices and context windows are counted in tokens, not words or characters. So everything above (the list size, step 0, the language, emoji, how numbers are cut) changes how much a request costs and how much text fits. Part 6.
